lesson.menu_title: What He Said in the Rehearsal
lesson.menu_desc: Passing the notes on without changing them -- reported speech for statements, questions and requests
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- What He Said in the Rehearsal
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 11 -- What He Said in the Rehearsal
lesson.grammar_point: reported speech: statements, questions and requests

listenings.text: I work between the musical director and the singers, and most of my job is passing notes on. The director talks fast, and he talks in shorthand. Last week he stopped the run-through and said, she is rushing the chorus again. If I walked over and repeated that, the singer would hear an accusation. So I told her that the band wanted a little more space in the chorus, and I asked her if she could sit back on the beat. Same note, different temperature. The second thing I do is check. When he asks me whether a singer is ready, I never just say yes. I go and ask her what she needs, and then I tell him exactly what she said, word for word, even when it is inconvenient. Once a contestant told me that she was scared of the key change. I reported that to the director, he moved the key down a step, and she nailed it on the night. Nobody in the audience knew. That is the job. You carry the message, and you make sure it arrives in one piece.

The worst note I ever passed on was four words long. The director came out of the control room and said, tell him to slow down. So I went to the drummer and told him to slow down. He did, and the whole song dragged. Twenty minutes later the director asked me why the drummer had changed the tempo. I said that he had told me to tell him to slow down. He looked at me and said that he had meant the singer, not the drummer. The singer was the one who was rushing. Nobody had asked who him was, because everybody thought it was obvious. Since then I have one rule. When somebody gives me a note for another person, I repeat it back before I walk away. I ask who it is for, and I ask what exactly they want to hear differently. It takes ten seconds, and it feels a little stupid. It is still the cheapest thing I do all day.

extra_audio.text: Marcus said that the verse was great. He told me that you were rushing the second chorus. He asked me to tell you to sit back on the beat. He asked whether you could sing the bridge an octave lower. He told us not to change the arrangement before Thursday. And I said that I would clarify the octave idea with him tonight.
